Issued at 1056 PM CDT Fri Sep 4 2026

Tonight through Saturday:

Water vapor imagery this evening shows the stalwart cutoff upper low 
spinning over the Pacific Northwest, propping up southwesterly flow 
over the Intermountain West that terminates in a ridge axis over the 
central CONUS. With another day of heat in the books, the attention 
in the near future now shifts to overnight/morning storm chances 
over parts of the NE/SD/IA vicinity, where already a swath of 
scattered cloud cover marks where forcing for ascent along the 
periphery of the LLJ is occurring. These clouds span from 
northwest Kansas into southeast South Dakota, the later of which
is where a best overlap of instability, dry lower levels with 
increase DCAPE, and forcing for ascent will exist. Sufficient 
instability will be in place for a few strong updrafts, but the 
maintenance of them could be difficult with minimal effective 
shear for them to avoid cold pool dominance. Recent runs of the 
CAMs have been a bit more tepid on how widespread the showers 
and storms will be, with several favoring the cluster across 
north-central SD to creep southward towards greater instability
before falling apart near the state line. Whether the develop 
in that area or drift in from the north, a 20-24% chance for 
storms exists for far northeast Nebraska, with only a 5% chance 
that a storm or two can reach strong to severe levels, maxing 
out between 5-8 AM. 

Once those storm chances simmer down we'll see soupy conditions 
manifest once again across the area, with widespread dewpoints 
remaining in the 70s while temperatures climb well into the 90s
during the afternoon hours. This does appear to the warmest day
of the forecast period, but with poor timing as many will be 
trying to enjoy outdoor gatherings on the front end of the 
holiday weekend. Heat indices are set to climb back into the 
100-107 degree range at their peak, with the highest values 
forecast over southwest Iowa and for the local metro areas. The 
tail end of a Heat Advisory carries through 7 PM tomorrow 
evening, with only slightly cooler temperatures expected going 
forward, so don't break out the fall sweaters just yet. 

A few scattered showers could cling to the nearby boundary set out 
by the morning convection across SD/northeast NE, with additional 
storms developing out west that drift towards us after 10 PM. Shower 
activity will likely increase overnight as convergence along the LLJ 
and leftover forcing from the decaying MCS to the west combine for 
rain chances covering eastern Nebraska. Once again, a low-end 
chance for severe storms exists for this activity (level 1 out 
of 5 risk for wind and hail), with the better chances focused 
west of the area. 

Sunday and Beyond:

Lingering showers from the overnight activity drifting in from the 
west will combine with additional activity from the north to make 
for a stormy morning and early afternoon, as several CAMs depict a 
more vigorous swath of storms moving across far eastern SD, into MN 
and western IA during the afternoon hours. Extended runs of the CAMs 
have featured strong wind gusts in their surface fields around 4 PM, 
which will likely necessitate an upgrade to the severe risk for 
Sunday. Mentioning these storms occur during the afternoon 
hours does bring the hope of a cooler evening as widespread 
convection interrupts our stagnant airmass while hopefully 
bringing some much- needed moisture to the recently dry area.

Monday through the rest of the week will start out with mid/upper 
heights falling slightly as the upper low out to the west begins its 
departure across far southern Canada, dragging a frontal boundary 
through the area Tuesday through Wednesday. The exact timing and 
speed of the passage will dictate shower and storm potential, with 
an afternoon passage spelling higher strong to severe storm 
potential as storms try to take full advantage of surface 
instability. By Thursday, global deterministic solutions suggest 
that this front will have pushed just to the south of the area into 
KS/MO, with a more uncertain fate for the boundary. Solutions have 
converged away from the GFS in depicting another slight ridge, while 
much of the other guidance suggests a more zonal (and therefore 
cooler!) pattern that grows with uncertainty towards the weekend.
